title: Go
subtitle: A small, fast, statically typed language built for networked services and the teams that maintain them, from a first program to professional practice.
description: Go is a compiled, garbage-collected language designed at Google and released as open source in 2009. It favours a small set of features that combine well, very fast builds, a single standard format for code, and concurrency built into the language with goroutines and channels. Much of today's cloud infrastructure is written in it, including Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform and Prometheus, along with countless web services, command-line tools and network programs.

This course is for anyone who already knows what a variable, a loop and a function are: the Start level of [Lumenary CS](/en/cs/) or equivalent experience in any language. It begins with installing Go and running a first program, covers the core language and its standard library, then the ideas that make Go distinctive (interfaces satisfied implicitly, errors as values, generics, goroutines and channels), and ends with testing, tooling and a complete small web service with JSON, written the way Go teams write it.

To run the code, download Go from [go.dev/dl](https://go.dev/dl/) (installers for Linux, macOS and Windows), or paste any program into the [Go Playground](https://go.dev/play/). Every complete program in these lessons was run by Lumenary's test suite with Go 1.27, and the output shown is the output it printed. The lessons were drafted with AI assistance and are awaiting review by a human computer scientist.

levels.title: Foundations
levels.summary: Install Go, organise code in modules, and learn the core language: types, control flow, functions with multiple results, and slices, maps and strings.

levels.title: Practice
levels.summary: Model data with structs and methods, abstract with small interfaces, handle errors as values, and write reusable code with generics and iterators.

levels.title: Professional
levels.summary: Write concurrent programs with goroutines, channels, sync and context; test, benchmark, fuzz and profile them; and build a small JSON web service the way Go teams do.
